NON-REPORTABLE 
 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 1785 OF 2024 
 
 
PRABHAVATHI REDDY RAVI 
AND RAVI PRABHAVATHI 
 
 … APPELLANT(S) 
  
VERSUS 
 
NALINI NERAIN AND 
OTHERS 
 
… RESPONDENT(S) 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
 
AUGUSTINE GEORGE MASIH, J. 
 
1. This appeal arises out of the final judgment and 
decree dated 25.07.2011 passed by the High 
Court of Judicature of Andhra Pradesh at 
Hyderabad (hereinafter referred as the “High 
Court”) in City Civil Court Appeal (C.C.C.A.) No. 
61 of 1990, whereby the High Court allowed the 
First Appeal filed by Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 

--- Page 249 ---
C.A. No.1785/2024 Page 2 of 8 
(defendants before the trial court) and set aside 
the judgment and decree dated 04.06.1990 
passed by the Additional Chief Judge, City Civil 
Court, Hyderabad (Temp.) (hereinafter referred 
as the “trial Court”) in O.S. No. 335 of 1983, 
which had decreed the suit for declaration of 
title and possession of vacant land measuring 
1350 sq. Yards, situated at Banjara Hills, Road 
No. 2, demarcated in the lay out as plot No. 3 
bearing Municipal No. 8-2-120/86/9 
(hereinafter referred as the “suit property”) in 
favour of the Appellant/Plaintiff. 
 
2. Brief facts are that the suit for declaration of 
title and possession filed by the 
Appellant/Plaintiff against the Respondent Nos. 
1 to 5 was decreed by the trial Court. It is 
pertinent to mention that the State of Andhra 
Pradesh was not made a party in the suit. 
Thereafter, during the pendency of the first 
appeal, the State of Andhra Pradesh instituted 
land grabbing cases against the parties and 
their predecessor-in-interest, culminating in an 
order dated 28.07.1993 of the Special Court in 

--- Page 250 ---
C.A. No.1785/2024 Page 3 of 8 
LGC No. 31 of 1991 and LGC No. 38 of 1991 
holding the suit property to be a Government 
land. After that, Writ Petition Nos. 15266, 
15268 & 14403 of 1993 filed against the order 
of Special Court were permitted to be withdrawn 
by a Division Bench of the High Court on 
14.07.2000, with an express observation that 
the findings of the Special Court and the 
observations made while permitting withdrawal, 
shall not come in the way of deciding the 
pending first appeal. 
 
3. Subsequently, the Division Bench finally heard 
the first appeal in 2011 and took a contrary 
view. The High Court suo motu impleaded the 
State of Andhra Pradesh and its officers as 
necessary parties, admitted the Special Court’s 
judgment as additional evidence, held the 
express observations of the earlier Division 
Bench's order to be per incuriam and allowed the 
appeal resultantly, dismissing the suit filed by 
the Appellant/Plaintiff on the grounds of clear 
findings of the Special Court that the suit 
property is Government land therefore, question 

--- Page 251 ---
C.A. No.1785/2024 Page 4 of 8 
of holding either parties (plaintiffs or 
defendants) as titleholders of the suit property 
does not arise. 
 
4. Having heard learned counsel for the parties 
and having perused the impugned judgment, we 
are satisfied that the matter need to be 
remanded to the High Court, for the reasons as 
follows. 
 
5. The High Court impleaded the State of Andhra 
Pradesh, the Collector, Hyderabad, and the 
Revenue Divisional Officer as respondents/ 
defendants under Order I Rule 10(2) CPC, 
holding them to be necessary parties for a 
complete adjudication of the question of title. 
Having so held, the High Court was obliged, as 
a matter of first principle, to issue notice to the 
newly added parties and afford them an 
opportunity of being heard before finally 
determining the very title dispute for whose 
adjudication their presence was found 
necessary. Instead, the appeal was disposed of 
finally on the date of allowing the impleading 

--- Page 252 ---
C.A. No.1785/2024 Page 5 of 8 
application itself, on the reasoning that no 
adverse orders have been passed against them. 
That reasoning does not answer the 
requirement of Order I Rule 10 CPC, the object 
of which is to enable the Court to effectually and 
completely adjudicate upon and settle all 
questions involved in the suit. An object that is 
defeated, if the newly added parties are never 
heard at all. 
 
6. Further, the judgment of the Special Court 
dated 28.07.1993 was received as an additional 
evidence in the appeal. This Court in Shalimar 
Chemical Works Limited v. Surendra Oil 
and Dal Mills (Refineries) and Others1 and 
other judgments have consistently held that the 
exception of Order XLI Rule 27 CPC is not 
intended to be used routinely and where 
additional evidence is admitted, the 
accompanying jurisprudence require that the 
party against whom it is used be given a fair and 
real opportunity to rebut it, whether by leading 
evidence or otherwise. On the facts as recorded 
 
1 (2010) 8 SCC 423 

--- Page 253 ---
C.A. No.1785/2024 Page 6 of 8 
in the impugned judgment itself, no such 
opportunity was extended to the appellant 
herein, before the Special Court Order was 
relied upon to conclude, finally and irreversibly, 
that she had no title to sue upon. 
 
7. We wish to clarify that we have not expressed, 
and should not be understood to have 
expressed, any opinion on the merits of the rival 
claims of title, or on the correctness of the 
findings of impugned judgment. Those are all 
matters that must be gone into afresh, on full 
hearing of all parties, by the High Court. 
 
8. In these circumstances, the impugned 
judgment dated 25.07.2011 in C.C.C.A. No.61 
of 1990 is set aside, and the appeal is remanded 
to the High Court for fresh disposal in 
accordance with law and in the light of the 
observations made above. It is directed that: 
a) Notice shall be issued afresh by the High 
Court to Respondent No. 11 - State of 
Telangana, who shall be permitted to file 
their written statement/counter and to place 
on record such material as they consider 
necessary; 

--- Page 254 ---
C.A. No.1785/2024 Page 7 of 8 
b) All parties shall be at liberty to lead 
additional evidence, if so advised, in relation 
to the judgment of the Special Court dated 
28.07.1993 and its effect, if any, on the 
question of title; 
c) All contentions of all parties on facts and in 
law, including on limitation, title, 
possession, the effect and binding nature (if 
any) of the land grabbing proceedings on the 
appellant, and on the merits generally, are 
left open. 
 
9. Given that the underlying suit was instituted 
several decades ago and the litigation has 
already travelled through the trial Court, the 
Special Court, writ proceedings and one round 
before this Court, the High Court is requested 
to make an endeavour to dispose of C.C.C.A. 
No.61 of 1990 as expeditiously as possible, 
preferably within 8 months from the date of 
receipt of this order. 
 
10. The appeal is allowed to the extent indicated 
above. 
 
11. There shall be no order as to costs. 
 

--- Page 255 ---
C.A. No.1785/2024 Page 8 of 8 
12. Pending application(s), if any, also stands 
disposed of.

1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Circuit

Bench at Kolhapur has rejected the prayers for grant
of  regular  bail  made  by  the  appellants,  Suhas
Appasaheb  Patil  and  Shrikrishna  Sawanta  Kabade.
While  Suhas  Appasaheb  Patil’s  application  was
dismissed  by  the  judgment  and  order  dated  11th
February,  2026,  the  application  of  Shrikrishna
Sawanta Kabade was dismissed exactly a month later,
by the judgment and order dated 11th March, 2026. 
3. These appeals take exception to such dismissal.
4. Both appellants figure as accused in FIR No.0157
of 2024 dated 30 th March, 2024 registered at Police
Station Sangli City, District Sangli, Maharashtra under
Sections 420, 406 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and Section 3 of the Maharashtra Protection of
Interest of Depositors (in Financial) Act, 1999. While
Suhas Appasaheb Patil was arrested on 30 th March,
2024,  Shrikrishna  Sawanta  Kabade  has  been  in
custody since 22nd December, 2024.
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
6. It  is  not  in  dispute  that  upon  completion  of
2

--- Page 258 ---
investigation, chargesheet has been filed on 17 th June,
2024. Prosecution proposes to record the evidence of
27  (twenty  seven)  witnesses  to  drive  home  the
charges against the appellants. Though charges have
been  framed  on  29th April,  2026,  but  not  a  single
witness has been examined. Thus, the trial is likely to
take some time to conclude. 
7. Appellants  –  Suhas  Appasaheb  Patil  and
Shrikrishna Sawanta Kabade – have been behind bars
for  quite  some  time.  They  have  no  criminal
antecedents.
8. Also,  accused  no.4,  i.e.,  Shankar  Rajaram,  has
been enlarged on bail by an order dated 04 th June,
2026; the appellants are, thus, entitled to claim parity.
9. T aking an overall view of the matter, we are of
the considered opinion that further detention of the
appellants pending trial is not necessary; and, since
the appeal deserves acceptance, the appellants may
be admitted to an order for grant of bail.
10. Accordingly,  we  set  aside  the  impugned

--- Page 259 ---
judgments and orders.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(@ S.L.P. (CRL.) NO. 9675 OF 2026)
MANJEET SINGH                 ...Appellant
VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & ORS.      ...Respondents
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant has been convicted by
the Trial Court for the offences punishable
under Section 120B and Sections 307 read
with 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
and  accordingly  sentenced  to  undergo
rigorous imprisonment for life with fine.
Pending his appeal against the same, the
1

--- Page 278 ---
High Court has rejected his application
for suspension of sentence. Aggrieved, the
appellant is before us.
3. We  have  heard  the  learned  counsel
appearing for the parties.
4. The learned counsel appearing for the
appellant submits that notwithstanding the
antecedents  of  the  appellant,  the  fact
remains that the appellant has been in
custody for a period of two and a half
years.
5. The learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-State submits that considering
the offences involved coupled with the fact
that  the  appellant  has  several
antecedents,  there  is  no  need  for
2

--- Page 279 ---
interference with the impugned order.
6. We  have  perused  the  antecedents  in
which the appellant is allegedly involved
and  find  that  most  of  the  cases  are
pertaining  to  small  offences.   In  the
present case also, the appellant has been
under custody for a period of about two
and a half years.  The appeal before the
High  Court  being  of  the  year  2025,
certainly,  substantial  time  would  be
required for its disposal. We also find
arguable  issues  in  the  appeal  pending
before the High Court, both on the facts
and the law. 
7. Suffice it is to state that continued
incarceration  of  the  appellant  is  not
3

--- Page 280 ---
required. In such view of the matter, we
are inclined to set aside the impugned
order passed by the High Court and suspend
the sentence of the appellant and grant
him bail pending his appeal before the
High Court. 
8. Accordingly, the impugned order is set
aside  and  the  sentence  imposed  on  the
appellant  stands  suspended  and  he  is
granted bail during the pendency of his
appeal  before  the  High  Court,  on  such
terms and conditions as may be imposed by
the concerned Trial Court.
9. Accordingly,  the  appeal  stands
allowed.
4

--- Page 281 ---
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

       (M.M. Sundresh)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.             OF 2026
[@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO.10714 of 2026]
MUKESH KUMAR                                   APPELLANT(S)
                           VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & ANR.                       RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         /2026
[@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL) NO.10724/2026]
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. These appeals impugn a common order dated 14.05.2026
passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at
Chandigarh whereby the bail granted by the court below
in connection with First Information Report (FIR)
No.100 of 2025 was set aside.
3. The prosecution case against the appellants, in a
nutshell, is that the appellants run a travel agency;
they promised a job in United States of America (USA)
to complainant’s husband and on that pretext, a sum of
Rs.50 lakhs was paid to the accused. However, instead
of sending complainant’s husband to USA, he was taken
to some other country whereafter he has gone missing.
The appellants were arrested in connection with the
aforesaid FIR. The matter was investigated and a
police report was submitted after investigation. The
1

--- Page 285 ---
appellants denied the allegations and applied for
bail. The Trial Court upon considering the nature of
allegations as also the statement made on behalf of
the  investigating  agency  that  custody  of  the
appellants is no longer required as investigation is
over, accepted the bail prayer of the appellants and
directed release of the appellants on bail.
4. Aggrieved by the bail granting order, the complainant
petitioned the High Court alleging inter alia that the
appellant - Manoj Kumar’s sister had approached the
complainant with an offer of Rs.40 lakhs but no
payment was made. It was argued before the High Court
that the appellants fraudulently obtained bail by
extending a carrot without any real intention to
fulfil the promise.
5. The High Court after considering the submissions of
the learned counsel for the parties, by the impugned
order set aside the bail order holding that the
concession of bail was obtained by deception i.e., by
promising repayment of the amount involved.
6. Aggrieved by the order of the High Court, these
appeals have been preferred.
7. The submission on behalf of the appellants is that the
lower Court granted bail not by relying upon any
2

--- Page 286 ---
promise allegedly made by the appellants but upon
consideration of the nature of the allegations and the
statement  made  by  the  investigating  agency  that
custody of the appellants is no longer required as the
investigation is over. It is submitted that, in such
circumstances, there was no justification for the High
Court to observe that the concession of bail was
obtained by deception i.e., by extending promise of
repayment of the amount involved.
8. It is also submitted that there is no finding returned
in the impugned order that the appellant had violated
any of the terms and conditions of the bail order. In
such circumstances, it has been argued, the High Court
committed manifest error in ordering cancellation of
bail.
9. On behalf of the respondent, it is submitted that it
is the admitted position that an offer to settle the
financial dispute was made during the proceedings
before the High Court. In such circumstances, the view
taken by the High Court that the bail was obtained by
deception cannot be faulted.       
10. We have considered the rival submissions and have
perused the materials available on record carefully.
From a perusal of the bail granting order of the lower
3

--- Page 287 ---
court, it does not appear that the bail prayer was
accepted on the promise to make a deposit by, or on
behalf  of,  the  bail  applicants.  The  bail  orders
indicate that the bail was granted on merits and upon
consideration  of  the  statement  made  by  the
investigating officer that investigation is complete,
and custody of the two accused is no longer required.
11. Besides, according to the learned counsel for the
appellants, the alleged offer to settle the dispute
was made by sister of one of the accused while the
accused was in jail; the same was made with a view to
get the criminal proceedings quashed; and that offer
was not made before the Court which granted bail.
Moreover,  there  is  no  such  recital  in  the  bail
granting order. 
12. At  this  stage,  we  may  observe  that  criminal
proceedings must not be used as a tool to coerce a
settlement.  Therefore,  while  considering  a  bail
prayer, the Courts must adhere to time tested legal
principles governing consideration of bail prayer and
desist  from  forcing  upon  the  bail  applicants  a
settlement. In our view, the High Court clearly fell
in error in interfering with the bail granting order
of the lower court.
4

--- Page 288 ---
13. At this stage, we may put on record that while issuing
notice on the petitions, on 03.06.2026, this Court had
recorded  the  undertaking  made  on  behalf  of  the
appellants that they would deposit a sum of Rs.10
lakhs within a period of two weeks in the Registry of
this  Court.  The  office  report  dated  31.07.2026
indicates that the two appellants have separately made
deposit of Rs.5 lakhs each pursuant to the said order.
In such circumstances, we deem it appropriate to
direct  refund  of  the  aforesaid  deposit  to  the
appellants  along  with  interest,  if  any,  accrued
thereupon.
14. For the reasons aforesaid, the appeals are allowed.
The order of the High Court setting aside the bail
order(s) passed by the Court below is hereby set
aside.  The  bail  of  the  appellants  shall  stand
restored.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

                   [MANOJ MISRA]
……………………………………………J

August 03, 2026

Non-Reportable 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No……………..of 2026
(@Special Leave Petition (C) No.7075 of 2021) 
Bahadur Singh (Deceased) Through LRs. & Ors. 
…. Appellants
Versus
Ram Kumar & Ors.
…. Respondent
O R D E R
Leave granted. 
2. The appellants before us, legal heirs of the original
judgment debtor, put forth a case of extreme hardship;
their valuable property having been sold in auction for far
less a price than the market value. The suit was filed by
the  second  respondent  bank  for  recovery  of  money  in
which a decree was passed and on execution, the property
was put up for auction by the Executing Court, Civil Judge
(Senior Division) Sirsa in Exe cution Petition No.23 of 1998.
The  first  respondent  purchased  the  property  for
Rs.5,25,000/-,  depositing  25%  of  the  auction  amount,
Rs.1,32,000/-,  upon  which  the  auction  was  confirmed
directing payment of the balance amount within 15 days.
The first  respondent,  auction  purchaser  deposited  the
balance amount, Rs.3,23,000/-, much later, vitiating the
Page 1 of 6
CA@ SLP (C) No.7075 of 2021 

--- Page 317 ---
sale in auction. The first respondent has a contention that
it was due to a clarification sought from the Court. The
borrower also raised objections with respect to the sale
conducted, pointing out that it was gross undervaluation
and  that  the  auction  was  vitiated  by  fraud  and
misrepresentation, rejected concurrently by the trial court
and in appeal. 
3. While the matter was pending before the High Court,
the  borrower  was  directed  to  hand  over  an  amount  of
Rs.11,52,000/- to the bank which was done. The Executing
Court was directed the release the land forthwith to the
original  owner  without  prejudice  to  the  rights  of  the
auction purchaser.  It is seen from the impugned order that
the auction purchaser had challenged that order up to this
Court, where, in a Special Leave Petition an order of status
quo was passed and later the SLP itself was dismissed for
non-prosecution.  However,  by  the  impugned  order,  the
High  Court  found  that if  third  party  rights are created,
payment of dues to the decree holder after creation of
such rights, cannot result in resumption of the property
and rejected the revision petition filed against the orders
of the Executing Court and the Appellate Court. 
4. We see from the orders of the Executing Court and
the First Appellate Court that the auction was upheld on
the  ground  that  the  judgment  debtor  did  not  file  an
application within 30 days from the date of the auction.
However, at the revisional stage, the High Court directed
the entire due amounts to be handed over to the bank
Page 2 of 6
CA@ SLP (C) No.7075 of 2021 

--- Page 318 ---
which was done by the petitioners before the High Court,
challenged unsuccessfully before this Court.
5. Before  us,  the  learned  counsel  for  the  appellants
agreed to pay reasonable interest to the first respondent
who is the auction purchaser.  The learned counsel for the
first respondent, however vigorously argued for rejecting
the  appeal,  especially  since  the  first  respondent,  now
aged, has been waiting all these years for the property,
which  by  sheer  of  passage  of  time  has  attained
astronomical value. The learned counsel appearing for the
bank fairly submits that their dues have been settled fully. 
6. Adjusting equities and balancing it, we have to notice
that as against the bid amount of Rs.5,25,000/- for the
entire land,  the borrower had deposited Rs.11,52,000/- in
2006 as directed by  the High Court in satisfaction of the
entire debt due to the bank. The auction was in 2003, and
the quantum of money deposited to save the land which
was auctioned,  three years later,  would clearly  indicate
that  it  was  very  much  undervalued  in  the  auction.
However, the fact remains that the first respondent had
paid the amounts in 2003, which is still remaining with the
Executing Court, the Civil Judge (Senior Division) Sirsa.  
7. We are of the opinion that interest of justice would be
served if the first respondent is granted simple interest at
the rate of 9 % per annum for the amounts deposited in
Court in the year 2003. The Executing Court shall compute
the interest payable as directed by us and shall, from the
total  amount payable deduct  the  amounts  deposited  in
Page 3 of 6
CA@ SLP (C) No.7075 of 2021 

--- Page 319 ---
Court  and  the  interest  accrued  thereat.  The  balance
amounts  shall  be  directed  to  be  deposited  by  the
appellants  herein  who  are  the  judgment  debtors/legal
representatives of the judgment debtor. On such deposit,
the  Bank  shall  release  the  property  to  the  judgment
debtor.  If  there  is  any  failure  to  deposit  the  balance
amounts  payable,  as  directed  by  the  Executing  Court,
there shall be a charge on the property and the amounts
remaining in Court with accrued interest shall be disbursed
to  the  respondent/auction  purchaser.  The  parties  shall
appear before the Civil Court (Senior Division), Sirsa on
18.08.2026.
8. The appeal stands disposed of on the above terms. 
9. Pending applications, if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

NON-REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.        of 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl) No.4577 of 2026) 
AVINASH ….  APPELLANT
(S) 
Versus
GOVIND TULSHYAN & ORS.        ….
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. The  appellant  is  the  complainant  on  whose  instance
Annexure      P-12, FIR was registered on 03.05.2024. The
appellant’s complaint was that the first accused arrayed in
the FIR along with five others, including the respondents
herein,  had  defrauded  him  of  Rs.4,15,00,000/-  (Rupees
Four crore and fifteen lakh) and despite an agreement by
the  first  accused  to  settle  the  issue,  nothing  has  been
done. 
3. The respondent Nos.1 and 2 approached the High Court
with  an  application  under  Section  482  of  Cr.P.C.  The
respondents’ contention was that they had no role to play
and it was the first accused who duped the complainant,
with whom the complainant had settled the matter. The
High  Court  having  extracted  the  FIR  and  also  the
Page 1 of 6

--- Page 323 ---
agreement  with  the  first  accused,  quashed  the  FIR  as
against the respondent Nos.1 and 2 finding that there was
nothing incriminating against the respondents and that in
any event there was an agreement entered into, to settle
the matter with the first accused.
4. We heard Sri K. Parameshwar, learned Senior Counsel for
the  appellant  and  Sri  S.  Nagamuthu,  learned  Senior
Counsel for the respondent Nos.1 and 2 and Sri Divyansh
Mishra, learned Counsel for the State.
5. Learned Counsel for the State submitted that there is a
definite money trail showing Rs.40,00,000/- (Rupees Forty
lakh)  and  Rs.15,000/-  (Rupees  Fifteen  thousand)  having
been deposited to the accounts of respondent Nos.1 and 2
respectively. The respondents do not have any explanation
for the said transaction. The money was also deposited by
the appellant herein. 
6. The clear case of the appellant is that the first accused
duped him under the pretext of procuring contracts and
took  around  Rs.4,15,00,000/-  (Rupees  Four  crore  and
fifteen  lakh),  which  the  complainant  had  transferred  to
various accounts and two payments have gone into the
accounts  of  respondent  Nos.1  and  2.  The  High  Court
accordingly  failed  to  notice  that  the  FIR  was  filed
subsequent to the agreement. The agreement as extracted
in the impugned order indicates the date to be 09.01.2024,
whereas  the  FIR  was  filed  on  03.05.2024.  It  has  been
categorically  recited  in  the  First  Information  Statement
that there was a settlement which was not complied with.
Page 2 of 6

--- Page 324 ---
7. Sri  S.  Nagamuthu,  learned  Senior  Counsel  for  the
respondent Nos.1 and 2, sought time to settle the matter,
at least  to  the  extent of  the  money  transferred  to  the
respondent Nos.1 and 2 herein.
8. We  cannot but notice that though  some  amounts were
transferred to the accounts of respondent Nos.1 and 2, for
which they have no explanation, the fact remains that the
allegation  in  the  complaint  itself  is  that  about
Rs.4,15,00,000/- were transferred to various accounts at
the  behest  of  the  first  accused.  In  the  circumstances,
repayment  of  the  amount  credited  to  the  respondents’
accounts would  not absolve them from criminal liability
since the complaint is of transfer of amounts far higher to
that transferred into the accounts of the respondents.
9. The High Court, as we observed, failed to notice that it was
on  the  failure  of  the  first  accused  to  comply  with  the
agreement that the FIR was lodged. The investigation also
detected  the  money  trail  to  the  accounts  of  the
respondents. 
10. We are of the opinion that the High Court erred in having
quashed  the  FIR  at  the  initial  stage  itself.  We,  hence,
reverse  the  order  of  the  High  Court  and  direct  the
investigation to be continued. The respondent Nos.1 and 2
shall appear before the Investigating Officer as and when
directed  to  appear  and  shall  co-operate  with  the
investigation. On the first appearance, the Investigating
Officer shall release respondent Nos.1 and 2 on bail on
such terms and conditions as he deems fit to impose. If the
respondent  Nos.1  and  2  do  not  co-operate  with  the
Page 3 of 6

--- Page 325 ---
investigation, then the Investigating Officer shall approach
the Magistrate Court to enable the arrest of the accused.
11. The Appeal stands allowed.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Writ Petition(Civil) No.708/2026 & W.P.(C) No. 829/2026 
1. By  these  writ  petitions  filed  under  Article  32  of  the
Constitution,  the  petitioners  have  prayed  for  the  following
reliefs: 
“a. Issue a writ, order, or direction, particularly in the nature
of a Writ of Mandamus, declaring Clause No. 16 of the Impugned
Advertisement  No.  18  of  2025  dated  08.08.2025  issued  by
Respondent No. 2 as ultra vires the Constitution of India, the
Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and the governing
service rules, and strike down the same as being unconstitutional
and void insofar as it restricts the benefit of reservation for
persons with benchmark disabilities to the domiciles/residents of
the State of Haryana;
b. Issue a writ, order, or direction, particularly in the nature
of a Writ of Mandamus, directing the Respondents to treat the
Petitioner's Application No. ADA05913 under the reserved category
for Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD) for recruitment to
the post of Assistant District Attorney, and to consider her
disability certificate dated 24.02.2023 as valid for all purposes
of the selection process irrespective of her domicile outside the
State of Haryana;
c. Issue a writ, order, or direction, particularly in the nature
of a Writ of Mandamus, directing the Respondents to modify the
online recruitment portal and recruitment procedure to ensure
that  all  eligible  persons  with  benchmark  disabilities,
irrespective of their domicile or residence, are permitted to
apply and compete against the seats reserved under Section 34 of

--- Page 342 ---
3
the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016;
d. And Pass such other or further order or orders as this
Hon'ble Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and
circumstances of the case.”
2. Today, when the matters were taken up for further hearing,
Shri  Siddharth  Iyer,  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
petitioners very fairly  brought to our notice that his client(s)
has/have not been able to clear the preliminary examination.
3. If  the aforesaid  be so, then the issues raised in these
petitions could be said to have been now become academic.  However,
having regard to the importance of the issues, we keep the
questions  of  law  open  to  be  agitated  in  some  appropriate
proceedings.
4. These petitions mainly concern the issue of domicile.
5. Mr. Lokesh Sinhal, the learned Senior Additional Advocate
General appearing for the State of Haryana has instructions  from
his client  to make a Statement before us that the State is
reconsidering  its  policy  of  restricting  reservation  for  PwBD
candidates only to domicile/resident candidates of the State of
Haryana, more particularly in light of the provisions of the Rights
of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.
6. The learned Senior Additional Advocate General has received
instructions in writing duly signed by Assistant District Attorney
(HRD) for Chief Secretary to Government, Haryana.
7. The communication in writing received by the learned Sr. AAG
is ordered to be taken on record.
8. In the wake of all these developments, as highlighted above,
we need not now adjudicate this petition further on merits.
9. We believe that it will be in the interest of one and all,
more particularly, having regard to the object and spirit of the
Act, 2016 that the State seriously  reconsiders its policy of
restricting the reservation for PwDA candidates only to admissible
residents/candidates of the State of Haryana.
10. With the aforesaid, these petitions stand disposed of.

W.P.(C) No. 804/2026:-
1. The petitioners have invoked  the  writ jurisdiction of this
Court under Article 32 of the Constitution and have prayed for the
following reliefs:-
(a) Issue an appropriate writ, order, or direction, preferably in
the nature of a Writ of Mandamus, declaring that the benefit of
horizontal  reservation  provided  to  Persons  with  Benchmark
Disabilities under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act,
2016 cannot be restricted solely on the basis of domicile,
residence, or permanent residency of a particular State or Union
Territory and that all Persons with Benchmark Disabilities are
entitled to compete for such reserved vacancies throughout the
territory of India irrespective of their State of domicile.
(b) Issue an appropriate writ, order, or direction, preferably in
the nature of a Writ of Mandamus, quashing and setting aside
Clause 16(1) and Clause 16(xi) of Advertisement No. 18/2025 dated
08.08.2025  issued  by  the  Haryana  Public  Service  Commission,
insofar as they restrict the benefit of reservation for Persons
with Benchmark Disabilities to residents/domiciles of the State
of Haryana.
(c) Issue an appropriate writ, order, or direction, preferably in
the nature of a Writ of Mandamus, quashing and setting aside
Clause 6(vi)(a) of Advertisement No. 13/2026 dated 25.02.2026
issued by the Bihar Public Service Commission, insofar as it
restricts the benefit of horizontal reservation for Persons with
Benchmark  Disabilities  only  to  candidates  who  are  original
residents of the State of Bihar.
(d) Issue an appropriate writ, order, or direction declaring that
any  rule,  recruitment  notification,  executive  instruction,
advertisement,  policy,  or  practice  issued  by  any  State
Government,  Union  Territory,  Public  Service  Commission,
recruiting agency, statutory authority, or instrumentality of the
State restricting the benefit of reservation for Persons with
Benchmark  Disabilities  solely  on  the  basis  of  domicile  or
residence  is  unconstitutional,  arbitrary,  discriminatory,  and
violative of Articles 14, 16,19, and 21 of the Constitution of
India as well as the provisions of the Rights of Persons with
Disabilities Act, 2016.
(e)issue an appropriate writ, order, or direction, preferably in
the nature of a Writ of Mandamus, directing the Respondents to
ensure that Persons with Benchmark Disabilities are permitted to,
avail the benefit of horizontal reservation in public employment
across aU States and Union Territories  irrespective  of  their
State of domicile or residence.
(f) Issue an appropriate writ, order, or direction declaring that
the  prescription  of  mandatory  prior  legal  practice  as  an

1. We are apprised by the learned counsel for the petitioner(s)
that Clauses (iv) and (v) of Paragraph 8 of the order dated
28.07.2026 require clarification, as they have, to some extent,
been misconstrued.

Clause (iv) of Paragraph 8 of the order dated 28.07.2026, the NCT
of Delhi or any other State shall be at liberty to take an
appropriate decision regarding the closure or withdrawal of the
FIRs lodged in various cases, in accordance with law.
3. Similarly, as regards Clauses (iv) and (v) of Paragraph 8 of
the order dated 28.07.2026, it is clarified that the expression
“criminal antecedents” appearing therein shall mean “grave and
heinous offences”.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL/INHERENT JURISDICTION
  Miscellaneous Application Diary No. 38217/2026
IN
Writ Petition (Civil) Diary No. 35746 of 2026
KARANARTHAM VIRAMAH FOUNDATION                     PETITIONER(S)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ANR.                        RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
  Miscellaneous Application No. 2221/2026
IN
Writ Petition (Civil) Diary No. 35746 of 2026
&
  Review Petition (Civil)   Diary No. 38333/2026  
IN
Writ Petition (Civil) Diary No. 35746 of 2026
O R D E R
1. I.A.  No.  215503  of  2026  in  Miscellaneous
Application  (Diary)  No.  38217  of  2026  seeking
permission to file application for recall of the
order dated 09.06.2026 is allowed.
1

--- Page 365 ---
2. The Union of India has moved this IA No.
184501 of 2026 seeking recall of the order dated
09.06.2026 passed in Writ Petition (Civil) Diary
No. 35746 of 2026. It is submitted by the learned
Solicitor General that the order under challenge
in the writ petition had already been set aside by
the Union of India, Ministry of Mines, Government
of  India,  vide its  order  dated  06.02.2026.
Therefore, as on the date of filing of the writ
petition, the order under challenge therein had no
existence. As such, the writ petition itself was
not maintainable.
3. It is also submitted by the learned Solicitor
General that neither the Union of India was made a
party in the writ petition, nor was the order
dated 06.02.2026 passed by the Ministry of Mines,
Government of India was brought to the notice of
this Court when the order dated 09.06.2026 was
passed.
4. Considering the factual position pointed out
by the learned Solicitor General, which is not in
dispute, and since the order dated 09.06.2026 was
passed  by  this  Court  at  the  mentioning  stage
without the other party having an opportunity to
point out the correct legal position and/or non-
existence  of  the  order  dated  14.01.2026,  the
recall application deserves to be allowed.
2

--- Page 366 ---
5. Learned Solicitor General would also submit
that the legal position as culled out by this
Court in the order dated 09.06.2026, of which
recall  is  sought,  has  huge  repercussions,  as
similar  matters  are  pending  in  several  High
Courts. Therefore, the benefit of the said order
must not inure to any of the parties.
6. In view of the above, we recall our order
dated 09.06.2026.
7. In the above circumstances, since the order
dated 14.01.2026 had no existence as on the date
of filing of the writ petition, the said Writ
Petition  (Civil)  Diary  No.  35746  of  2026  was
infructuous  from  day  one.  As  such,  nothing
contained in our recalled order dated 09.06.2026
shall inure to the benefit of any of the parties
in the writ petition or in this miscellaneous
application.
8. Accordingly, Miscellaneous Application (Diary)
No. 38217 of 2026 stands allowed. The order dated
09.06.2026 is recalled, and Writ Petition (Civil)
Diary No. 35746 of 2026 is taken on board and
dismissed  as  infructuous.  Nothing  contained  in
this order shall inure to the benefit of any of
the parties.
9. Miscellaneous Application No. 2221 of 2026 is
dismissed as infructuous.
3

--- Page 367 ---
10. In view of the dismissal of Writ Petition, the
Review  Petition  does  not  survive  for
consideration.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) No. 27136 of 2023)
HANSA JAIN … APPELLANT
VERSUS
VINOD KUMAR SANGHAI (DECEASED) THR. 
LEGAL REPRESENTAIVES & ANR. … RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Being aggrieved by an ex parte granted on 12.10.2018, the
appellant had preferred an application under Order IX Rule 13
which was rejected vide order dated 06.01.2020. On filing a
civil revision, it was also dismissed vide order impugned on
06.10.2023.  Being dissatisfied by both these orders, the
present appeal has been filed.
3. On issuing notice, the landlord tendered appearance and
filed counter affidavit. On 28.11.2025, direction was issued
to file the details of the arrears and rent till date.
Thereafter on 05.12.2025, this Court passed an order in the
proceedings which is as under :

--- Page 371 ---
2
“1) Apropos previous order, the statement
of dues of rent has been filed by the
petitioner as well as the respondents.
2)  Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioner
contends  that  the  rent  is  due  from
November,  2021,  and  prior  to  the  said
period, rent has already been paid in the
account of Mr.Vinod Kumar Sanghai (since
deceased)  (husband  of  the  landlady).
Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
respondents wishes to verify the said fact.
The bank account details produced along
with the special leave petition be verified
by the respondent who shall revert on the
same by filing an affidavit within four
weeks.
3) In the meantime, as per the calculation
placed before us by the respondent, a sum
of Rs.15,44,762/-is due up to December,
2025, adding escalated rent in terms of the
agreement.  The  petitioner  is  ready  to
deposit the said amount within the time as
directed by this Court. 
4) In view of the above, we postpone the
hearing of this case till 23.01.2026. The
petitioner  shall  deposit  a  sum  of
Rs.15,44,762/- with the Registry of this
Court  which  shall  be  kept  in  interest
bearing  short  term  fixed  deposit  of  a
nationalised Bank on auto renewal basis.
5) The respondent shall verify the bank
account statement and file an affidavit
ascertaining  about  the  deposit  and
informing if the deposit is not made by the
petitioner.
6) List on 23.01.2026.
7) Interim order to continue till then.”

--- Page 372 ---
3
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that they have
deposited the rent as directed till the end of May, 2026 which
is disclosed in the affidavit calculating Rs.16,000/- per
month adding 5% escalated rent every year.  The amount of Rs.
15,44,762 has been deposited on 22.01.2026 which is lying in
an interest bearing fixed deposit and the remaining rent from
January to May, 2026 of Rs.4,01,445/- has been deposited by
the appellant on 18.05.2026 and it is kept in a non-interest
bearing account.  As such the amount of the arrears of rent
till May, 2026 has been deposited subject to verification by
the landlord.
5. After hearing learned counsel for the parties at length
and considering the facts, wherein the ex parte was proceeded
within 33 days from the date of service and the judgment has
been pronounced immediately and within 32 days, as urged even
without lapse of the statutory period for filing the counter
affidavit  granting  decree  of  eviction,  in  our  view,  a
reasonable opportunity of hearing ought to be given to the
appellant to put his defence.  Therefore, we set aside the ex
parte decree and allow the application under Order IX, Rule 13
of Civil Procedure Code, 1908.
6. In consequence, the suit be restored to its file in its

--- Page 373 ---
4

GAJJALA YOGANAND                              Appellant(s)

O R D E R
1. This  appeal  impugns  an  order  of  the  National
Company  Law  Appellate  Tribunal  (NCLAT)  dated
30.04.2016 whereby IA No.601/2025 in Company Appeal
(AT) (CH) (Ins) No.217/2025 was rejected. 
2. The appellant is a personal guarantor of credit
facility  availed  by  a  corporate  entity  named
Manjeera  Retail  Holdings  Pvt.  Ltd.  (for  short
’MRHPL’-CD). On failure of CD to repay its debt,
personal  insolvency  resolution  process  under
Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code,
2016 (for short, ‘IBC’) was initiated against the
appellant by M/s Catalyst Trusteeship Limited (the
respondent) i.e., the assignee creditor. By Order
dated 11.03.2025, the National Company Law Tribunal
1

--- Page 377 ---
(for short, ‘NCLT’) had admitted the insolvency
resolution petition. Against the order of admission
of the petition, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins)
No.217 of 2025 was filed before NCLAT.
3. In that appeal, the appellant moved an application
for stay, which came to be rejected by the impugned
order. 
4. According to Mr. Neeraj Kishan Kaul, the learned
senior counsel appearing for the appellant, the
stay application was heard on 25.04.2025 and orders
were reserved. The impugned order rejecting the
stay application was passed on 30.04.2026. It is
submitted that while passing the impugned order,
NCLAT  had  failed  to  consider  multiple  key
submissions; such as, for the very same loan of
which the appellant was a personal guarantor, one
Manjeera Construction Ltd. (for short, ‘MCL’) was a
corporate guarantor; petition(s) under Section 7 of
IBC were filed both against MRHPL and MCL. On the
Section 7 petition against MRHPL, a resolution plan
was approved making a provision for the claim set
out by the creditors including the respondent who
2

--- Page 378 ---
were  paid  thereunder;  in  consequence,  the
respondent did not press its claim against MCL
i.e., the corporate guarantor. It is contended that
those developments indicated that there was no
justification to proceed in the personal insolvency
resolution process initiated against the appellant
by the respondent. The grievance of the appellant
is that all these aspects were not considered by
NCLAT while rejecting the stay application. 
5. Shri Krishnendu Datta, learned senior counsel who
appears for the respondent, submits that it is
incorrect to state that the respondent is paid off
completely; the dues payable to the respondent are
in excess of 60 crores as on date and as there was
no stay on the admission of the petition under
Section  95,  in  the  meantime,  resolution
professional has been appointed who has invited
claims, and claims in excess of 300 crores have
already been submitted. In such circumstances, it
is not a fit case where this Court should interfere
with the order rejecting the stay application.
6. We have accorded due consideration to the rival
3

--- Page 379 ---
submissions. What surprises us is the lack of
discussion in the impugned order regarding the
subsequent  developments  which  have  been  placed
before us. Perhaps the long period for which the
order was reserved, as stated, might be the reason
for those aspects escaping consideration in the
impugned order. Be that as it may, we do not wish
to elaborate on that. However, since we notice that
there is no consideration of all the above aspects
while rejecting the interim application, we deem it
appropriate to set aside the order of NCLAT and
restore the interim application (I.A. No.601 of
2025) on the file of the pending appeal for a fresh
consideration by NCLAT in accordance with law,
preferably, within one month from the date a copy
of this order is placed before NCLAT. 
7. The appeal is allowed in the above terms. The
impugned order dated 30.04.2026 passed on I.A.
No.601 of 2025 is set aside. I.A. No. 601 of 2025
shall stand restored on the file of Company Appeal
(AT) (CH) (Ins) No.217 of 2025 for being considered
and decided afresh before consideration of the main
appeal provided appeal is not decided already.

Non-Reportable
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.8906 of 2012
Municipal Corporation
of City of Ahmedabad
Thr. Commissioner     ….Appellant
Versus
Asim Chemical Industries
(Now known as Crystal Quinone
Pvt. Ltd. Thr. Its Proprietor) & Anr.            
….Respondents
W I T H
Civil Appeal No.8907 of 2012
O R D E R
Both  the  appeals  are  concerned  with  the  issue  of
liability  to  property  tax;  whether  an  allottee  can  be
mulcted with that liability prior to his possession.
2. Learned Senior Counsel for the Municipal Corporation,
who  is  the  appellant  herein  contended  that  the  Court
completely misinterpreted Section 140(3) of the Gujarat
Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949. Section 140(3)
was interpreted to find that no dues of property tax can
be  levied  on  the  petitioners  for  more
than one year. It is the contention of the Corporation that
Page 1 of 5

--- Page 393 ---
such restriction does not apply to owners and it applies
only to the occupiers.
3. We see from the order that the Corporation’s Counsel
had  conceded  before  the  High  Court  that  the  original
petitioners  before  the  High  Court,  i.e.  the  respondents
herein  came  into  possession  of  the  property  only  on
20.01.1993 and the property tax demanded is from that
date i.e. for one year. The impugned order noticed the said
concession  and  hence  found  the  provisions  of  Section
140(3) did not permit the appellant herein to recover any
amount  of  property  tax  from  the  respondents  herein
remaining due for more than one year.
4. On perusal of the Act of 1949, an ‘owner’ has been
defined as any person who receives the rent of the said
premises  or  who  would  be  entitled  to  receive  the  rent
thereof and an ‘occupier’ as a person who for the time
being is paying or is liable to pay to the owner the rent of
any  portion  of  land.  Section  139  which  identifies  the
person who has the liability to pay speaks of various kinds
of leases including those from the Government/Corporation
etc.
5. In the present case an industrial plot was allotted by
the  Gujarat  Industrial  Development  Corporation  on
07.09.1992  and  it  was  possessed  by  the  petitioner  on
20.01.1993. There is no clarity as to whether the persons
are inducted as lessees or absolute owners and even if
Page 2 of 5

--- Page 394 ---
inducted as lessees whether they are permitted to sublet
the premises.
6. In the above circumstances, we are of the opinion
that the impugned judgment is not liable to be interfered
with and the same has to be sustained, but the question of
law as to the interpretation of Section 140(3) is kept open.
Refund as directed shall be paid with two months from the
date of this order.
7. The appeals stand disposed of.
8. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.

(Cardiology).The promotion, shall, however, take effect
in  accordance  with  the  applicable  rules  and  only  on
notional basis as far as its retrospectivity is concerned.
The petitioner shall not be entitled to draw the higher
pay  of  the  promotional  post  until  his  actual  date  of
promotion.”
3. The “immediate junior” of the first respondent, referred to
in the above extract, are two doctors. If the order of the High
Court  were  implemented,  they  would  stand  superseded.
However, they were not parties to the proceedings either
before  the  Tribunal  or  the  High  Court.  In  our  considered
opinion, the High Court erred in making a direction of the
nature noticed above without hearing them.
4. It  is  only  on  this  short  ground  that  we  set  aside  the
impugned judgment and order, and remit the writ petition
for  fresh  consideration  by  the  High  Court  in  the  manner
indicated hereafter.
5. The  first  respondent  shall  file  an  application  for
impleadment  of  the  said  two  doctors.  Upon  impleadment
being allowed and notices being served, the writ petition
may be decided afresh in accordance with law and upon
granting  opportunity  of  hearing  to  the  impleaded
respondents as early as possible.
6. Since the matter has been pending for quite some time,

--- Page 399 ---
3
we  request  the  roster  Bench  to  decide  the  writ  petition
within a year, however, subject to its convenience.
7. The civil appeal is disposed of, accordingly.
8. All points and contentions on merits are kept open.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.

Pradesh under Section 34(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Excise
Act, 1915 (as amended).
5. The prosecution case is that following a search

1

--- Page 403 ---

subject  to  the  appellant  co-operating  with  the
investigation.
7. In the hearing today, on a query, learned counsel for
the appellant submits that though appellant has written to
the Investigating Officer, he has not yet been summoned in
connection with the investigation of the aforesaid case.
8. Opposing the prayer for anticipatory bail, learned
counsel for the respondent-State of Madhya Pradesh submits

upon conviction.

absolute.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 12461 of 2026)
VED PRAKASH AHUJA   APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
ABHAY PRAKASH AHUJA RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. In a suit for eviction pending since 2012,
wherein the appellant, presently aged about 93
years, had his examination concluded in the year
2016, the defendant moved an application seeking
re-examination  of  the  appellant,  by  moving
application (Exhibit 577) seeking production of
the original agreement dated 20.12.1972 and for
his cross-examination on that document.
3. The Trial Court rejected the application
(Exhibit  577),  however,  in  a  petition  under
Article 227 of the Constitution of India, the
High  Court,  under  the  impugned  order,  has
interfered and set aside the Trial Court's order,
directing  the  appellant’s  examination  by
directing him to produce the original of the
1

--- Page 408 ---
agreement dated 20.12.1972.
4. Shri Shyam Divan, learned Senior Counsel,
would submit that the appellant/plaintiff having
closed his examination and the defendant also
having examined six of his witnesses, at this
stage  the  appellant  cannot  be  compelled  to
produce a document and present himself for cross-
examination once again. He would submit that the
Trial Court may apply appropriate principles of
evidence, including drawing of adverse inference
against the party who is denying to produce any
document, however, compelling a witness aged 93
years  to  get  himself  re-examined  with  the
document after more than 10 years of closure of
his deposition is not proper.
5. Mr. Atmaram Nadkarni, learned Senior Counsel
appearing  for  the  respondent/defendant,  would
submit that if the appellant is ready to face the
consequences for his inability to produce the
original of the agreement, the trial may proceed
on that basis.
6. In view of the statements made by learned
counsel for the parties as recorded above, we
dispose  of  the  application  (Exhibit  577)
preferred by the respondent/defendant before the
Trial Court by observing that the appellant’s
unwillingness to produce the original of the
2

--- Page 409 ---
agreement  dated  20.12.1972  may  attract  the
applicable  principles  of  law  of  evidence,
including the principle of drawing of adverse
inference, and that the appellant is not required
to produce the document or submit himself to re-
examination.
7. Accordingly,  the  order(s)  passed  by  the
Trial Court and the High Court are set aside.
8. I.A.  Nos.  164981/26  and  164982/26  are
disposed of. 
9. The Appeal is disposed of in the above
terms. 
10. The interim order(s) passed by this Court
are vacated, and the Trial Court is directed to
proceed with the trial and conclude the same at
the earliest.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

was  an embezzlement of the  amounts  collected. It  is  also  the  case  of  the
prosecution that after payment of NCPUL registration fee and limited deposit
into the society’s account, the remaining amount was dishonestly retained and
misappropriated by the appellant. Despite notice and demand for explanation
and deposit, the same has not been deposited by the appellant.
1                                                                                                     SLP(CRL.) NO.9612 OF 2026

--- Page 423 ---
5.  However,  it  is  defence  of  the  appellant  that  said  amount  was  adjusted
towards  scholarships  granted  to  students  and  he  has  relied  upon  emails,
representations,  bank  deposits,  income-expenditure  statements  and  list  of
scholarships, which is stoutly denied by the learned counsel appearing for the
complainant. It is contended  that on receipt of notice from the Investigating
Officer (IO) and aforesaid defence taken up by the appellant, the society has not
been able to demonstrate as to how the said plea was incorrect or without any
basis.
6. The correctness of these rival contentions, would not be in the realm of
consideration by this Court at the time of considering the prayer for grant of
bail. T ravelling in this path would be dangerous and may adversely affect the
rights of either of the parties. Hence, we desist from doing so.
7. This Court while issuing notice on 25.05.2026 had granted interim protection
subject to appellant cooperating with the investigation. It is also not in dispute
that subsequent to the order passed by this Court, the IO has summoned the
appellant and appellant has appeared and appears to have been singing the
same song without any change in his tune according to prosecution. If it were to
be so, it cannot be expected that the accused is required to answer the question
posed by IO in the manner in which the IO requires. It is for the trial court to
evaluate the evidence to arrive at a conclusion for the correctness of rival
contentions.
8. In the light of there being no flight risk and appellant is appearing before the
IO, we deem it proper to make the interim order absolute.
9.  Accordingly, appeal is allowed. Impugned order is set aside. Appellant is
ordered to be released on bail on such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional
IO may deem fit to impose and also on the condition that appellant would
appear before the jurisdictional trial court on all dates of hearing except when
2                                                                                                     SLP(CRL.) NO.9612 OF 2026

--- Page 424 ---
exempted for any specific reason.
10. We also make it clear that in the event of there being violation of any of the
conditions, the State as well as complainant, would be at liberty to move the
jurisdictional court for cancellation of bail, if they so desire.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

and after fullfledged trial appellant came to be convicted
by Judgment dated 16.07.2025 and sentenced to ten years
rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees

Criminal Appeal No. 3550/2026                             1

--- Page 438 ---
4. Being  aggrieved  by  the  same,  appellant  has
preferred Criminal appeal No. 1531/2025 before the High

without going into the contentions raised for suspension of
sentence and the grounds urged in support of the same.
Hence, this appeal.

any  opinion  on  the  merits,  since  the  appeal  is  to  be

Court to expedite the hearing.

disposed of.

--- Page 457 ---
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.                OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (C) NOS. 25184–25185 OF 2024)
KRISHI UPAJ MANDI SAMITI DHAR  ...Appellant
                                VERSUS
PRESTIGE AGRO TECH LIMITED & ORS.     ...Respondents
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Aggrieved by the impugned order dated 03.01.2024
passed by the Division Bench of the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh, by which the writ appeal filed by respondent
No.1 was allowed and the cancellation of the license of
respondent No.1 along with the consequential penalty was
set aside, the appellant is before us.
3. The  learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant,  while  assailing  the  impugned  judgment,
submitted before us that there is no privity of contract
between the appellant on the one side and the respondent
Nos.5 and 6 on the other. License has been issued by the
appellant only to respondent No.1. Thus, it is this
respondent  which  has  to  pay  the  Mandi  fees.  The
respondent No.1 had sought for exemption from payment of
Mandi  fees  by  submitting  forged  and  fabricated
1

--- Page 458 ---
declarations that the fees had already been paid by the
sellers, i.e., respondent Nos.5 and 6. When the show
cause notice was issued to respondent No.1, it did not
even dispute the forged documents but put onus on the
appellant and raised a plea that, for the wrong committed
by respondent Nos.5 and 6, it cannot be made to suffer.
He further submitted that the Division Bench of the High
Court, while considering the definition of “Commercial
Transactions”, vis-a-vis Section 19 read with Section 33
of the M.P. Krishi Upaj Mandi Adhiniyam, 1972, has
wrongly reversed the order of the learned Single Judge.
4. The learned counsel appearing for respondent no.1
submitted that there is no need to interfere with the
impugned judgment, particularly, when in the teeth of the
definition of “Commercial Transactions”, it is for the
appellant  to  verify  the  record  and  proceed  against
respondent Nos.5 and 6.
5. We are not inclined to give our imprimatur to the
impugned order passed by the Division Bench of the High
Court. Undoubtedly, there is no privity of contract
between the appellant on one side and the respondent
Nos.5 and 6 on the other. In fact, it is the specific
case of respondent No.1 that respondent Nos.5 and 6 are
the licensees of different Mandis wherein the requisite
fee had been paid and that there is no need for further
2

--- Page 459 ---
payment to the appellant.
6. Factually, there is no dispute that payment of Mandi
fees has not been made to the appellant. The respondent
No.1 has not challenged the finding on fact that the
documents produced were forged and fabricated. It is the
respondent No.1, who being a licensee, has to pay the
requisite amount otherwise. The said respondent produced
the fabricated documents in order to get an exemption
from the payment of the Mandi fees. The view expressed by
the High Court cannot be sustained in the eye of law as
the definition of “Commercial Transactions” will not
apply in the case at hand wherein the transactions are
not between two licensees. The authority that issues the
license has also got the power to cancel and revoke the
same. Looking from this perspective, we are not inclined
to give our imprimatur to the impugned order passed by
the Division Bench of the High Court.
7. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to restore
the order of the learned Single Judge. However, while
restoring the order of the learned Single Judge insofar
as the cancellation of license is concerned, we find that
there  is  no  clear  finding  on  the  willfulness  of
respondent No.1 as it is yet to be ascertained as to
whether respondent No.1 was responsible for the same or
respondent Nos.5 and 6. We are not on criminal liability.
3

--- Page 460 ---
Thus, the consequence of cancellation of license as
against the imposition of penalty stands on a different
footing  which  must  involve  the  willfulness  of  the
defaulting party. 
8. Taking note of the above, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order passed by the Division Bench
only insofar as the setting aside of penalty is concerned
which shall be duly paid by respondent No.1, excluding
the Mandi fee.  
9. Accordingly, the Civil Appeals stand allowed in the
above terms. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
………………………………………………………J.
      (M.M. Sundresh)
………………………………………………………J.
       (Prasanna B. Varale)
New Delhi;
July 27, 2026.

pre-arrest bail, an order came to be passed on 25th May, 2026 by the High Court

United States of America. In view of the impending expiry of the Green Card on
11th November, 2026 and the serious consequences that could ensue in terms
of invalidation of such card, if the petitioner does not return to the USA prior to

the subject matter of challenge in this special leave petition.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Having  heard  the  learned  counsels  appearing  for  the  parties  and  Mr.
Pitambar Acharya, learned Advocate General appearing for the State, in the
peculiar facts of the case, we are not inclined to interfere with the impugned
order. 
2. However, we hasten to add that the course adopted by the learned Single
Judge to arrive at a conclusion that Communicative English is also called as a
core subject in English or Economics being called as Business Economics in
B.Com Degree, which was the mandate of the advertisement, would amount to
substituting the view of the Court to that of the employer who invited the
applications from the candidates by prescribing the criteria. This by no stretch
of imagination can be construed as the hyper-technical approach as opined by
learned Single Judge. It is for the authorities to arrive at a conclusion as to
whether any subject is equivalent or not. Additionally, we may add that subject
Economics, even if it takes its purview from the subjects of Macro-Economics or
Micro- Economics, no inference can be drawn that the Business Economics is
the same subject as that of Economics or Industrial Chemistry being equivalent
to core Chemistry and similar subjects. The Courts cannot sit in the arm chair of
the experts to decide the equivalency. Even otherwise, it is for the employer to
3

--- Page 497 ---
decide as to what is equivalent, even assuming it for the sake of arguments,
they can be construed as equivalent even if it has been so construed by any
University.
3. As such, confining this finding only to the facts obtained in the present case
and holding that this shall not construed as precedent and in the peculiar facts
of the case, we dismiss the Special Leave Petitions.
4.  We make it clear that this order is confined to the candidates who had
approached the High Court and pursued their grievance up to this Court in the
present Special Leave Petitions only and would not extend to fence sitters.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
     CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.1397-1398 OF 2010
ZONAL MANAGER LIFE INSURANCE
CORPORATION OF INDIA ETC.           APPELLANTS
                                VERSUS
DEPUTY INSPECTOR GENERAL
REGISTRATION/DEPUTY COMMISSIONER,
STAMPS ETC.           RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1.  Mr. N. Venkataraman, learned Additional Solicitor
General, at the outset, has drawn the attention of this
Court towards the judgment delivered in the case of Life
Insurance Corporation of India vs. The State of Rajasthan
and Ors. (Civil Appeal No.3391 of 2011) 2024 INSC 358
involving the same controversy.
2.  The record of the case reveals that the judgment
rendered in the aforesaid case was related to State of
Rajasthan whereas the present case pertains to the State
of Uttar Pradesh.  This Court in the aforesaid case in
paragraphs 37 and 38 has held as under: 
37. Therefore, having considered the matter in
detail, we finally hold that:
I. The preliminary issue relating to the
applicability of the relevant state law,
i.e., the 1952 Act or the 1998 Act, is
answered by holding that the Rajasthan
Stamp Law (Adaption) Act, 1952 applies to
the present case.
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.1397-1398 OF 2010

--- Page 503 ---
2
II. We hold that the state legislature has
the legislative competence to impose and
collect  stamp  duty  on  policies  of
insurance under Entry 44 of List III, as
per the rate prescribed by the Parliament
under Entry 91 of List I.
III. We hold that for the execution of
insurance policies within the state of
Rajasthan,  the  appellant  is  bound  to
purchase India Insurance Stamps and pay
the stamp duty to the state of Rajasthan.
IV. While we have upheld the power and
jurisdiction of the state to levy and
collect stamp duty on insurance policies,
in the facts and circumstances of the case
as indicated hereinabove, we direct that
the state government shall not demand and
collect the stamp duty as per the orders
dated 16.09.2004, 16.10.2004, 11.10.2004,
01.11.2004, and 28.10.2004.
38. In conclusion, we dismiss the appeals and
affirm the judgment of the High Court dated
21.02.2011 in D.B. Civil Special Appeal (Writ)
No. 670 of 2004, D.B. Civil Writ Petition No.
3418 of 2006, D.B. Civil Writ Petition No.3419
of 2006, D.B. Civil Writ Petition No.3420 of
2006 and D.B. Civil Writ Petition No.8187 of
2004. We also set aside certain findings of the
High Court to the extent indicated in issue no.
IV and direct the State Government not to
demand and collect stamp duty as per the orders
dated  16.09.2004,  16.10.2004,  11.10.2004,
01.11.2004, and 28.10.2004.”
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.1397-1398 OF 2010

--- Page 504 ---
3
3. In the considered opinion of this Court and in
the light of the aforesaid judgment, the order passed by
the High Court deserves to be upheld and is accordingly
upheld.  However, it needs to be modified to the extent
that the stamp duty which is being demanded and collected
by the State Government shall not be collected as per the
demand from the Life Insurance Corporation of India in
respect  of  the  period  in  question.   The  learned
Additional Solicitor General of India has also pointed
out that a Bank Guarantee has been furnished by the Life
Insurance Corporation of India and the same be returned
to the Life Insurance Corporation of India. It is ordered
accordingly.
4.  The Civil Appeals stand dispose of.
5.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 17 OF 2026
EXPRO NORTH SEA LIMITED PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
HINDUSTAN OIL EXPLORATION 
COMPANY LTD & ANR.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The  instant  petition  filed  under  Section  11(6)  of  the
Arbitration  and  Conciliation  Act,  1996  (Act),  seeks  the
appointment of a Sole Arbitrator to adjudicate disputes arising
out of the Operation and Maintenance Contract dated 29.05.2019
(O&M Contract) executed between the Petitioner and Respondent
No.1 for providing operation and maintenance services for the
Mobile Offshore Production Unit (MOPU), which is a mobile
offshore oil/gas production facility, located at Key Gibraltar
in the Mumbai Offshore Basin. 
2. Briefly observed, the Petitioner, a company duly incorporated
under the laws of the United Kingdom, was engaged under the O&M
Contract to operate and maintain the production equipment
installed on the MOPU. Respondent No.1 subsequently entered
into an Assignment Agreement dated 19.06.2023 with Respondent
No. 2, transferring its rights, title and obligations under the
O&M Contract to Respondent No. 2. Thereafter, on account of the
1

--- Page 507 ---
stated operational difficulties, Respondent no. 1 issued a
notice of termination of agreement dated 01.04.2025. 
3. Due to the aforesaid termination, it appears that disputes
arose between the parties concerning, inter alia, non-payment
of the outstanding dues claimed by the Petitioner, as well as
the Petitioner’s removal from the MOPU operations and the
subsequent takeover thereof by the Respondents. The Petitioner
thereafter  claimed  outstanding  dues  aggregating  to  USD
1,913,715.37 and other contractual claims arising out of the
termination. The Respondents, on the other hand, denied bearing
any outstanding liabilities to the Petitioner. 
4. Owing to this, the Petitioner issued a notice of arbitration
dated  29.08.2025  under  Clause  20.2  of  the  O&M  Contract,
nominating Hon'ble Ms. Justice Chitra Venkataraman (Retd.) as
the Sole Arbitrator. The Respondents did not agree to the
proposed appointment, prompting the Petitioner to file the
instant Arbitration Petition. 
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
material placed on record. 
6. Having regard to the facts and circumstances recorded above and
the relevant provision(s) under the  O&M Contract, we deem it
just and proper to allow the instant Arbitration Petition and
appoint Hon'ble Mr. Justice R. Suresh Kumar, former Judge of
the Madras High Court, as the Sole Arbitrator to adjudicate the
2

--- Page 508 ---
disputes  between  the  parties.  The  seat  and  venue  of
arbitration, in accordance with the arbitration agreement,
shall be Chennai, India.
7. We make it clear that the parties will be at liberty to raise
all available contentions before the learned Sole Arbitrator.
8. The learned Sole Arbitrator shall have the liberty to fix her
own remuneration/fees. Ordered accordingly.
9. Pending interlocutory applications, if any, also stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

SHYAM EPC PVT. LTD RESPONDENT(S)

ARBITRATION PETITION NO. 49 OF 2025
O R D E R
1. These three petitions have been filed under Section 11(6) read
with Section 11(12) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act,
1996 (1996 Act). The petitioner is a company incorporated in
Bhutan, whereas the respondent is an Indian company. 
2. The  petitions  concern  three  Engineering,  Procurement  and
Construction  contracts,  all  dated  01.12.2022,  relating
respectively to civil construction; supply; and erection,
installation, testing and commissioning for a 2 x 33 MVA Ferro
Silicon Project in Bhutan.
3. Notably, each of the three contracts contains an arbitration
clause  providing  for  resolution  of  disputes  through
arbitration. It is further discernible that the agreed place
1

--- Page 511 ---
of arbitration is New Delhi and the arbitral proceedings are
to be governed by the 1996 Act.
4. Briefly, disputes are stated to have arisen between the
parties in relation to the performance of the three contracts.
It is submitted that the petitioner terminated all three
contracts by notice dated 16.12.2024 and, by a consolidated
notice dated 10.03.2025, invoked arbitration in respect of the
disputes arising thereunder. Further, the respondent did not
act upon the invocation notice, leading to the institution of
the present petitions.
5. Notice was issued in these matters, and pursuant to the order
dated 20.03.2026, substituted service was effected on the
respondent through publication in  Sakshi and  The Times of
India. Despite completion of service, no one has appeared on
behalf of the respondent.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner and perused
the  material  placed  on  record.  The  existence  of  the
arbitration agreements and the respondent's failure to act
upon the invocation notice are sufficiently borne out from the
record. The petitions are, accordingly, allowed.
7. Hon'ble Mr. Justice Mukul Mudgal, former Chief Justice of the
Punjab and Haryana High Court , is appointed as the Sole
Arbitrator in all three matters to adjudicate the disputes
2

--- Page 512 ---
between the parties arising out of the three EPC contracts
forming the subject matter of these petitions.
8. The seat and venue of arbitration shall be New Delhi, in
accordance with the arbitration agreements.
9. We clarify that this Court has not expressed any opinion on
the merits of the disputes. All factual and legal contentions
of the parties, including their claims and counterclaims, are
left open to be raised before the learned Sole Arbitrator.
10. The learned Sole Arbitrator shall be at liberty to determine
his fees and other terms in consultation with the parties.
11. Pending  interlocutory  applications,  if  any,  also  stand
disposed of.

order is not to be construed as imposing a blanket prohibition on
the reporting of court proceedings by recognised news outlets. Such
outlets may, therefore, continue to report on the proceedings and
inform the general public of legal developments and judicial
pronouncements, save that audio or video clips of the court
proceedings shall not be utilised in the course of such reportage.
In sum, while news outlets may continue to report on the court
proceedings,  they  shall  nonetheless  remain  bound  by  the
restrictions set out in paragraph 10.
3. Accordingly,  paragraph  11  of  our  earlier  order  dated
24.07.2026 stands clarified to that extent.
4. IA No.219940/2026 (application for intervention) is allowed.
The applicants are permitted to assist this Court as intervenors.  
5. Learned counsel for the respondents seek and are granted four
weeks' time to file counter affidavit.  
6. List on 18.09.2026.

3. Having gone through the records, we are of
the opinion that there is no reason why we should
interfere with the reasoned judgment of the High
Court which finds clinching evidence to hold the
appellant/accused guilty of the offences alleged
against him. However, we notice that the trial
court had sentenced the appellant to 4 years of
rigorous  imprisonment  while  the  High  Court

i.e., rigorous imprisonment for a period of 3
years, the impugned order of sentence is also
1

fact the trial court had awarded a sentence of 4
years of rigorous imprisonment.
4. From the observations of the High Court, we
understand that the High Court was of the opinion
that the case required only an award of minimum
sentence, which is 3 years. Hence, we clarify that
the sentence as awarded by the trial court, of 4
years of rigorous imprisonment will stand modified
to  3  years  of  rigorous  imprisonment.  The
imposition of fine and default sentence, if any,
would be as ordered by the trial court.

modifications.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       /2026
   [SLP [C] NO.24461/2023]
SULTAN MIA                          Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
ZAHIR MIA & ORS.                     Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  counsel
appearing for the appellant and the learned counsel
appearing for the respondents.
Learned  Senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant  would  submit  that  the  High  Court  had
completely misconstrued the scope of Section 47 of
the  Code  of  Civil  Procedure,  1908  (hereinafter
referred to as ‘the Code’). The suit was instituted
decades ago. Much water has flown under the bridge.
The suit was filed for partition. It is further
submitted  that  the  High  Court  had  exceeded  its
jurisdiction in setting aside a preliminary decree,
which is even beyond the scope of Section 47 of the
Code.
Learned counsel appearing for the respondents
submitted that the decree being a nullity, the High
Court had rightly arrived at its conclusion.

--- Page 535 ---
2
We are inclined to record certain facts.
Respondent Nos.1 to 4 claim their rights on the
basis that they are the legal heirs of the deceased
defendant No.30. However, the suit stood dismissed as
against defendant No. 30. She died after the judgment
had been reserved but before it was pronounced. 
We are not inclined to examine whether the case
would attract Order XXII Rule 4(4) of the Code.
Suffice it to state that both the Trial Court and the
High  Court  erred  in  passing  the  orders  under
challenge.  While  deciding  an  application  under
Section 47 of the Code, the Court is required to
adjudicate the issues raised therein, the scope of
the provision being fairly wide.
In other words, such an application cannot be
disposed of merely on the ground of delay or by
recording a finding that the decree is a nullity,
without  deciding  the  issue  that  arise  for
consideration.
In such view of the matter, we are inclined to
set aside the orders passed by the Trial Court as
well as the High Court, though for different reasons.
The application filed under Section 47 of the
Code is restored to the file of the Trial Court. The
Trial Court is directed to decide all the issues
arising therein, uninfluenced either by the earlier
proceedings or by any observations made by us in this

--- Page 536 ---
3
order.
Appropriate orders shall be passed within a
period of eight weeks from the date of receipt of a
copy of this order.
The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
………………………………………….J.
[M.M. SUNDRESH]
………………………………………….J.
[PRASANNA B. VARALE]
NEW DELHI;
